concepts.subject: physics
concepts.misconception: I think mass and weight are the same quantity; both use the kilogram
concepts.misconceptionSource: seed probe misconception-tagged choice (verbatim, first-personed)
concepts.correctTyped: No — the KILOGRAM is the SI base unit of MASS (how much matter). WEIGHT is a FORCE — the gravitational pull on that mass, F = mg — and forces are measured in newtons (N), a derived unit. A 70 kg person has a weight of about 686 N on Earth (g ≈ 9.8 m/s²) and about 114 N on the Moon (g ≈ 1.6 m/s²) — same mass in kg, different weight in N. "My weight is 70 kg" mixes the two quantities; "my mass is 70 kg" is the precise statement
concepts.wrongTyped: Yes — mass and weight are the same quantity; both use the kilogram
concepts.typedSource: seed probe ""My weight is 70 kg." Is the kilogram the unit of weight?" (isCorrect choice / misconception-tagged choice, verbatim)
concepts.offTopic: Every physical quantity is essentially a number — you can add temperature, time and force the same way. Is that right, or does something depend on more than a number?

concepts.subject: physics
concepts.misconception: I think all physical quantities are just numbers; direction is a description, not a quantity
concepts.misconceptionSource: seed probe misconception-tagged choice (verbatim, first-personed)
concepts.correctTyped: No — some quantities need a DIRECTION as well as a magnitude, and they combine differently for it. Two 5 N forces in the SAME direction give a net 10 N; two 5 N forces in OPPOSITE directions give net 0 N; two 5 N forces at right angles give ~7 N at 45°. Same magnitudes, three different physical outcomes — scalars alone (temperature, time, mass) cannot produce that. Force, displacement, velocity, acceleration and momentum are vectors precisely because direction changes the physics
concepts.wrongTyped: Yes — all physical quantities are just numbers; direction is a description, not a quantity

concepts.offTopic: A car is cruising at a constant 60 km/h on a level road. To keep going at constant speed, does the engine have to provide a NET forward force on the car?

concepts.subject: physics
concepts.misconception: I think the force of the throw is still in the ball
concepts.misconceptionSource: EB phys.mech.newtons-first-law misconception "Motion needs force ("what keeps it moving?") — the impetus model" symptom
concepts.correctTyped: No — a car at constant velocity has ZERO net force on it. The engine's forward push exactly BALANCES friction plus air drag: F_engine = F_friction, so ΣF = 0 and a = 0 (which is exactly what "constant velocity" means, by Newton's second law). The engine is not providing a net force to "maintain motion" (that would be a Newton-first-law violation — Aristotelian intuition); it is providing the force needed to CANCEL the resistive forces that would otherwise slow the car down
concepts.wrongTyped: Yes — to keep moving at constant velocity the car needs a constant net forward force from the engine
concepts.typedSource: seed probe "A car is cruising at a constant 60 km/h on a level road. To keep going at consta" (isCorrect choice / misconception-tagged choice, verbatim)
